claims.text: Separately computing lattice and electronic thermal conductivity will improve prediction accuracy for HfNbTaTiZr relative to approaches that combine the contributions.
The target material includes nearly perfect, defect-free bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The target material also includes HfNbTaTiZr containing a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen addition.
The lattice contribution can be calculated from first-principles phonon dispersion and anharmonic scattering with Debye-temperature corrections.
The electronic contribution can be derived independently from analytical or data-driven electron-transport estimates.
The proposed model is applicable over approximately 200–1300 K.
Below 200 K, electronic heat transport dominates in HfNbTaTiZr.
Below 200 K, the proposed decoupling approach becomes less applicable and requires additional electron-transport modeling.
Phonon lifetimes and dispersion mediate the lattice thermal-transport response.
Electronic band-structure features affect electron mobility and electronic thermal transport.
Previous approaches contain a conflation error because they do not adequately separate lattice and electronic thermal conductivity.
DFT-derived phonon dispersion and anharmonic corrections produce more accurate phonon-scattering rates.
Independent electronic-transport estimates avoid oversimplified coupling between lattice and electronic contributions.
The proposed approach will improve prediction accuracy by approximately 20–30% relative to earlier models.
The approach will correctly reproduce temperature-dependent variation in thermal transport.
The approach will correctly reproduce changes in thermal transport caused by controlled oxygen impurity levels.
Existing analytical estimates often assume perfect, defect-free crystals and do not fully resolve independent lattice and electronic scattering mechanisms.
The approach is less reliable for heavily defected or microstructurally complex samples.
Neutron or X-ray scattering and Hall measurements can provide independent tests of the predicted phonon and electronic transport quantities.

The hypothesis is falsified if separate lattice and electronic predictions differ from independently measured values by more than ±30% over 200–1300 K, or if the total prediction does not significantly outperform earlier approaches.
